The Geometry of Dependence

Theory, Chapter 2

theory-02-geometry-of-dependence.Rmd

The space where cover data live

Cover data do not live in ordinary space. When we record the proportions of five species in a plot, we do not have five independent numbers that could each take any value. We have five numbers that must be non-negative and must sum to one. This constraint defines a specific region: a four-dimensional surface embedded in five-dimensional space.

This changes what the data are.

In unconstrained space, each dimension is independent of the others in a structural sense. A point can move freely along any axis without affecting its position on the other axes. The axes are orthogonal not just geometrically but logically: knowing the value on one axis tells you nothing about possible values on the others.

On a constrained surface, this independence disappears. A point cannot move freely in all directions. Movement in one direction forces compensating movement in others. The dimensions are coupled by the constraint itself, before any data are observed and before any biological process is invoked.

Why constrained spaces induce dependence

Consider a plot with five cover categories: grasses, forbs, shrubs, bare ground, and litter. The five proportions must sum to one. Suppose grasses currently occupy 40% of the plot. What can we say about the other categories?

The remaining four categories together occupy exactly 60%. If grasses increase to 50%, the total available to all other categories drops to 50%. If grasses occupy 80%, forbs, shrubs, bare ground, and litter together can occupy at most 20%, regardless of their individual tendencies or how they were measured.

A logical consequence of the constraint, not a correlation estimated from data or a biological interaction between plant functional types. The cover of grasses restricts the possible covers of every other category, and vice versa, because all draw from the same finite total.

The same logic applies to any pair of components in any compositional dataset. Knowing the value of one component constrains the possible values of all others. This induced dependence exists regardless of how the data were generated, how many observations we have, or whether the components interact in any meaningful biological sense.

The impossibility of independent components

In unconstrained settings, asking whether two variables are independent is meaningful. We can imagine a data-generating process where each variable is determined by its own separate mechanism, with no connection between them. Independence is a coherent hypothesis that could be true or false.

For components of a composition, the question is malformed. Independence would require that knowing the value of one component tells us nothing about the possible values of another. The sum constraint guarantees that it does. If species A occupies 80% of a plot, all other species together occupy exactly 20%. Information the constraint imposes.

One might object: perhaps independence holds in some underlying latent space, before the constraint is applied. A reasonable line of inquiry, and later chapters will examine what can and cannot be said about latent structure. But it does not rescue component-wise thinking at the level of observation. The data we observe are the constrained proportions, not the latent quantities. Whatever independence might hold in an underlying unconstrained space, the observed components remain dependent. The constraint transforms independent latent variation into dependent observed variation.

This is why “testing for dependence” among cover components is conceptually confused. The dependence is guaranteed. The question is not whether it exists, but what form it takes beyond the minimum the constraint induces.

Negative correlations without interaction

Compositional structure causes components to be negatively correlated, even when no process drives them apart.

Consider the simplest case: a plot with only two categories, species A and bare ground. These two covers must sum to one, so they are perfectly negatively correlated. If species A has high cover, bare ground must be low. This correlation is not estimated; it is determined.

With more categories, the pattern is less rigid but persists. Generate compositional data by any reasonable process and compute correlations among components: negative correlations will dominate. Not because the components are competing. Because they draw from the same finite pool.

A researcher who observes negative correlations among species covers might interpret this as evidence of competitive exclusion. In some cases, it may be. Compositional structure alone, however, guarantees some negative correlation. Separating the geometric effect from the biological effect requires understanding what dependence the constraint induces. Impossible if the constraint is ignored.

Why marginal thinking fails

Much of applied statistics operates marginally: consider one variable at a time, or pairs of variables, and build up understanding from these components. For compositional data, this approach is unreliable.

The marginal distribution of a single cover component (species A considered in isolation) does not tell us how species A behaves in the composition. Species A might have high variance marginally but low variance conditionally on the other components. It might appear symmetric marginally but be highly skewed in context. The marginal view is incomplete.

Pairwise relationships are equally misleading. The correlation between species A and species B depends on what else is in the composition. Add a third species with high and variable cover, and the correlation between A and B will change. Not because their relationship changed, but because the geometric context changed. Pairwise correlations are not stable properties of the components; they are artifacts of the full compositional structure.

Standard multivariate methods, which often assume that marginal or pairwise information is sufficient, cannot be trusted for compositional data. The constraint couples all components simultaneously. Understanding one or two at a time misses the structure.

The constraint is not a nuisance

Tempting to treat the sum constraint as an inconvenience, something that complicates analysis but can be managed with appropriate adjustments. This view is mistaken.

The constraint is not separate from the data. It defines what the data are. A vegetation plot with 30% grass, 25% forbs, 20% shrubs, and 25% bare ground is a single object: a partition of space. The four numbers are not four independent measurements that happen to sum to one. They are four aspects of one thing.

Attempting to remove the constraint (by dropping one component, by using ratios, by transforming to an unconstrained space) does not make the dependence disappear. It relocates the dependence into a form that may be harder to see but is no less present. The structure of the constrained space follows the data into whatever representation we choose.

What this means

Dependence in cover data is not a hypothesis to be tested or an effect to be estimated. A structural fact imposed by the nature of the measurement. Any two components of a composition are dependent, necessarily, because they share a common bound.

This dependence is geometric. It arises from the constraint, not from species interactions, environmental filtering, or ecological dynamics. These biological processes may add further structure, but they operate on top of a dependence that is already guaranteed.

Ignoring this geometry does not make it go away. It makes the analysis incoherent. A model that treats cover components as independent has not made a simplifying assumption. It has made a false statement about what the data are.

This vignette does not propose a solution. It establishes that the problem exists and cannot be avoided. Any serious treatment of cover data must begin by accepting that the components are coupled, and that this coupling is not optional.
